title: Nash equilibrium
objectives: Find the pure equilibria and say why neither player wants to move.

screens.title: Both on a best reply
screens.prose: The first table of lesson 1. Ana chooses the row and Ben the column; each cell is (Ana's payoff, Ben's payoff), in £. Green marks Ana's best replies and amber Ben's.

state.caption: Ana's best replies and Ben's best replies.

screens.question: Tap every cell where both players are playing a best reply.

hints.text: Look for a cell marked twice.
Ana's marks are U in L, D in C and M in R.
Only (D, C) is in Ben's set too.

feedback.correct: (D, C) = (3, 3): it is a best reply for both.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Tap only cells that are in both players' sets.

byKey.anas: You tapped Ana's best replies. Ben must be on a best reply too, and he is only in (D, C).
byKey.bens: You tapped Ben's best replies. Ana must be on a best reply too, and she is only in (D, C).

explain.text: Only (D, C) wears both marks. There D is Ana's best reply to C and C is Ben's best reply to D. Each is doing the best they can against the other.

screens.title: Nobody moves alone
screens.prose: A cell where both play a best reply is a **pure Nash equilibrium**. Check it: Ana may change her row while Ben stays at C.
screens.question: From (D, C), what is the most Ana can earn by switching rows alone, in £?

hints.text: Ben stays at C, so Ana moves within column C.
Column C gives Ana 0 at U and 2 at M.
The best switch pays 2, less than the 3 she has.

feedback.correct: £2, by moving to M: less than her £3 at D.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep Ben at C and read Ana's payoffs down column C.

byKey.four: The 4 is at (M, R). Reaching it needs Ben to move too, which a switch alone does not allow.
byKey.stay: £3 is what she has at D. Switching gives at most 2.

explain.text: Moving to U or M earns Ana 0 or 2, less than 3. Ben moving to L or R earns 2 or 1, less than his 3. Neither gains by moving alone, which is what the equilibrium promises.

screens.title: Two venues
screens.prose: Two desks each post a large order on venue X or venue Y. Both on X pays (3, 3), both on Y pays (1, 1), and apart (0, 0), in £1,000.
screens.question: Tap every pure Nash equilibrium.

hints.text: Test each cell: would either desk gain by moving alone?
At (Y, Y), a desk moving to X alone drops from 1 to 0.
(X, X) and (Y, Y) both hold.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check every cell for a gain from moving alone.

byKey.best: (X, X) is better for both, but (Y, Y) holds too. From it, each alone would drop to 0.
byKey.worst: (Y, Y) holds, but so does (X, X), where both earn 3.

explain.text: At (X, X) and at (Y, Y) a desk that moves alone drops to 0. Both are equilibria, although both desks prefer (X, X). An equilibrium is stable, not necessarily good.

screens.title: A race for a block
screens.prose: Two traders race for a block trade, each Aggressive or Passive. Both aggressive: each loses £2. One aggressive: that trader makes £4 and the passive one £0. Both passive: £3 each.
screens.question: Tap every pure Nash equilibrium.

hints.text: Test (Passive, Passive) first: does Ana gain by turning aggressive?
From (P, P), turning aggressive pays Ana 4, more than 3.
The equilibria are the two cells where exactly one trader is aggressive.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check every cell for a gain from moving alone.

byKey.pp: (P, P) pays 3 each, but Ana gains 1 by turning aggressive: 4 > 3.
byKey.pp3: (P, P) does not hold: Ana gains 1 by turning aggressive, 4 > 3.

explain.text: From (P, P) either trader gains 1 by turning aggressive. From (A, A) either gains 2 by backing off to 0. Only the two lopsided cells hold, each with one aggressive trader.

screens.title: The best cell
screens.prose: The two desks of lesson 2: each quotes Tight or Wide, with (Ana, Ben) in £1,000 a day.
screens.question: Tap every pure Nash equilibrium.

hints.text: From (Wide, Wide), would Ana gain by switching alone?
Switching to Tight pays Ana 5, more than 4.
Only (Tight, Tight) holds.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check each cell for a gain from moving alone.

byKey.ww: Both earn more there, but each gains by switching alone: 5 > 4.
byKey.two: (Tight, Tight) holds, but (Wide, Wide) does not: each gains by switching alone, 5 > 4.

explain.text: (Wide, Wide) has the largest total, but from it Ana gains by switching to Tight, 5 against 4. Ben gains the same way. An equilibrium is about moving alone, not about the best cell for the pair.

screens.title: Matching pennies
screens.prose: Matching pennies at £1: Ana wins £1 from Ben when the coins match, and Ben wins £1 when they differ.
screens.question: Where is the pure Nash equilibrium?

options.why: Ben loses £1 there, so he switches to Tails.
Ana loses £1 there, so she switches to Tails.
In every cell someone loses £1 and would switch.

hints.text: In each cell, who lost the round?
The loser can always switch and win.
So no cell holds.

feedback.correct: None: whoever loses a round wants to switch.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for the player who wants to move in each cell.

explain.text: Every cell has a loser, and the loser gains £2 by switching. So no cell is an equilibrium in pure moves. Lesson 4 finds one by mixing.

screens.title: Pure Nash equilibrium
screens.prose:
What you tapped: a cell where Ana's payoff tops its column and Ben's tops its row.

$$a_{i^*j^*} \ge a_{ij^*} \text{ for all } i, \qquad b_{i^*j^*} \ge b_{i^*j} \text{ for all } j$$
screens.question: A cell is Ana's best reply but not Ben's. Is it a pure Nash equilibrium?

options.text: No: Ben gains by changing his column
Yes: one best reply is enough
options.why: Both conditions must hold. Ben would move, so the cell does not last.

options.text: Yes, if its total is the largest
options.why: Totals play no part. Ben gains by moving alone, so it fails.

hints.text: Who would move from that cell?
Ben is not on a best reply.
So Ben moves: not an equilibrium.

feedback.correct: No: both must be on a best reply.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Both conditions must hold.

explain.text: If Ben is not on a best reply, some other column pays him more. He moves, and the cell is gone. Both conditions are needed, and the totals of the cells never enter.

screens.title: Drill
screens.prose: Three new games, about three minutes each, as an interview allows. Say the reasoning aloud before you answer. Slide through the games; no best replies tie.
screens.question: Count the pure Nash equilibria.

rows: The venue game: (3, 3) on X, (1, 1) on Y, (0, 0) apart

hints.text: Mark Ana's best reply in each column and Ben's in each row; count the cells marked twice.
Game 2: Ana's marks are M in L, B in C, B in R; Ben's are C, C, C.
0, 1 at (B, C), 2 at (T, C) and (M, L), and 2.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first answer that is marked.

byKey.r0c1: Game 1: Ana's marks are B in L, T in C, T in R; Ben's are L, C, R. No cell has both.
byKey.r1c1: Game 2: only (B, C) = (6, 6) is marked for both.
byKey.r2c1: Game 3: (T, C) = (3, 5) and (M, L) = (6, 4) are both marked twice.
byKey.r3c1: The venue game has two: (X, X) and (Y, Y).

explain.text: Game 1 has none: Ana's marks (B, L), (T, C), (T, R) miss Ben's (T, L), (M, C), (B, R). Game 2 has one, (B, C); game 3 has two, (T, C) and (M, L). The venue game has two.

screens.title: Follow-up: the spread table
screens.prose: The interviewer returns to the spread table of lesson 1. The tighter quote gets 100 lots, a tie splits them, and each lot earns £1 per tick.
screens.question: Tap every pure Nash equilibrium.

hints.text: Test each cell on the diagonal first.
At (2, 2), undercutting to 1 tick earns Ana £100, the same as she has.
(1, 1) and (2, 2) hold; at (3, 3) undercutting earns £200 against £150.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check each cell for a strict gain from moving alone.

byKey.tight: (2, 2) holds too: undercutting to 1 tick earns £100, a tie, so nobody gains.
byKey.wide: (3, 3) fails: undercutting to 2 ticks earns £200 against £150.
byKey.thr: At (3, 3) Ana gains by undercutting to 2 ticks: £200 against £150.

explain.text: At (2, 2) undercutting to 1 tick earns £100, the same as staying, so nobody gains by moving. At (3, 3) undercutting earns £200 against £150, so it fails. A tie keeps an equilibrium, so competing quotes can stop at two ticks as well as at one.

ideas: Mark every best reply of both players; a cell marked for both is a pure Nash equilibrium.
At an equilibrium neither player gains by moving alone; a tie still holds.
A game can have several equilibria, or none in pure moves, as in matching pennies.

formula.name: Pure Nash equilibrium
formula.note: Best in its column for Ana, best in its row for Ben.

summary.trap: Tapping the cell with the largest total. Ask whether either player gains by moving alone.

quiz.prose: The spread table: (Ana, Ben) in £, by the ticks each quotes.
quiz.question: Why is (3 ticks, 3 ticks) not an equilibrium?

options.text: Ana gains by undercutting to 2 ticks: £200 against £150
Both earn less there than at (2, 2)
options.why: They earn more at (3, 3), £150 each against £100. It fails because one undercut pays.
There is no wider quote here. The gain comes from undercutting to 2 ticks.

feedback.correct: Undercutting by one tick pays £200, more than £150.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for a move one player gains from alone.

explain.text: At (3, 3) each earns £150. Ana moving to 2 ticks wins all 100 lots at £2: £200. A strict gain from moving alone breaks the equilibrium.

quiz.prose: A new game: Ana chooses the row and Ben the column; each cell is (Ana's payoff, Ben's payoff), in £.
quiz.question: How many pure Nash equilibria does it have?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Mark Ana's best reply in each column and Ben's in each row.

byKey.one: Check your cell. Ana's marks are B in L, T in C, B in R. Ben's are L in T and C in B.
byKey.two: No cell is marked for both. Ana's marks are (B, L), (T, C), (B, R); Ben's are (T, L), (B, C).

explain.text: Ana's best replies are (B, L), (T, C) and (B, R). Ben's are (T, L) and (B, C). No cell is in both sets, so there is no pure equilibrium.

quiz.prose: In some cell of a game, Ana could gain £1 by changing her row alone. Ben could gain nothing by changing his column.
quiz.question: Is that cell a pure Nash equilibrium?

options.why: Both must be on a best reply. Ana gains by moving, so the cell does not hold.

options.text: Yes: £1 is too small to matter
options.why: Any strict gain counts. Ana moves for £1.

feedback.correct: No: Ana is not on a best reply.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Neither player may gain by moving alone.

explain.text: An equilibrium needs both players on a best reply. Ana gains £1 by moving, so she is not. No switch may pay strictly more, so a tie, as at (2, 2) in the spread table, still holds.
